pages.h1: Websites and booking for a new barbershop in Lombard, IL.
pages.lede: A shop that opened last month and a shop that's held the same corner for twenty years look almost identical on a phone screen. The difference is that one of them has a hundred people vouching for it.

sections.h2: Ninety days is how long you get to stop being the new place.
paras: The lease is signed, the chairs are in, and the part nobody warns you about starts the morning after. For that first stretch you're invisible in every way that counts — no reviews, a listing that says almost nothing, and a shop name nobody has ever typed. None of that is a verdict on your cutting. It's a verdict on how little the internet currently knows about you.

So the first three months get treated as their own piece of work, with an order to it. The listing goes up properly, the site goes live with real prices, the booking button works from day one, and every person who sits down gets asked for a review. Then it keeps happening, week after week, until the whole thing stops looking freshly opened.
bullets: The Google listing verified and held in your own account, not somebody else's
Photographs of your room, your chairs and your own work instead of a stock interior
A price list a stranger can read without ringing to ask
Booking open the week you open, not the month you get around to it

sections.h2: Your first forty haircuts matter more than the next four hundred.
paras: Each one is somebody who took a chance on a shop with nothing to go on. Ask while the cape is still on and most of them will leave a review that same evening. Miss that window and you're back to hoping.

On Growth the asking runs by itself — a short message after the cut, in words you'd actually use, sent to everybody rather than to whoever you happened to remember on a quiet afternoon. A listing that gains reviews steadily reads as a shop people go to. A listing frozen at four reads as a shop that might not be there any more.

sections.h2: An old shop gets found by memory. A new one gets found by search.
paras: The man who's been on the block two decades has customers who drive to him without deciding anything. You can't buy that and you can't rush it. What's available to you is the search that happens when somebody moves into the area, or finally gets one bad cut too many somewhere else, and types a haircut and a town into a phone.

That search is winnable. It comes down to a profile filled in the whole way, pages that name the cuts you do in the words people use for them, and a site that opens fast on two bars of signal. There's nothing clever in any of it. It just has to be done, every week, by somebody whose job it is.

sections.h2: A stranger asks different questions than your regulars do.
paras: Your regulars already know you take walk-ins after three and that a kid's cut is quicker on a weekday. A first-timer knows none of it, and every unanswered question is a reason to tap back and try the next result. Say whether walk-ins are welcome. Say what a fade costs, what a beard costs, and what it comes to if he wants both.

Put the parking on the page. Say what happens if he turns up ten minutes late. It reads like ordinary housekeeping and it works as reassurance, which is the one thing a new shop is genuinely short of.

sections.h2: What it costs while you're getting known.
paras: Two plans, both numbers here rather than behind a phone call. Foundation is $250 each month with $250 once at the start, and covers the site on a domain in your name, the Google Business Profile built out properly, booking tied to your Google Calendar, email at your own address, the local search work, and a couple of changes a month whenever you ask for them.

Growth is $500 each month with $500 at the start, and switches on the review requests, the client ledger, the automatic texts and emails, card payments, expense tracking and a monthly report. Pay a year ahead and 15 percent comes off, so the twelve months land at $2,550 or $5,100 with the build fee kept separate. Either plan can carry round-the-clock call answering at $100 a month, or review replies at $130.

sections.h2: Open Knox Chops and book yourself in.
paras: Knox Chops is a barbershop we built the whole way through, and the booking on it is live. Take a slot the way a customer would, then look at what the counter sees when you do. It settles the question this page can't, which is whether the thing underneath the writing is any good.

pages.townPara: The platform at 9 S. Main Street sits 19.9 miles from Ogilvie, which makes Lombard the closest to the city of the towns we work in. That distance turns up in the barbering. Plenty of people here spend the working week somewhere else entirely and do their choosing on a phone — at seven in the morning, or at half six at night with a seat and nothing else to do. A new shop isn't competing for a glance through a window. It's competing inside a search made by somebody who has twenty-five minutes to fill.

crmCallout.heading: A client list you own, starting from the very first cut.
crmCallout.para: The letters stand for customer relationship management, which in a barbershop means one list of names with dates beside them. From week one it holds who came in, who cut them, what they paid and roughly when they'll want another. A shop three months old has no history at all, so the sooner something starts writing it down, the sooner you've got something worth owning. It's registered to you, and it leaves when you leave.

cta.heading: Judge the work rather than the pitch.
cta.para: Project Knox is new, and we'd rather say that on our own page than let you find it out in month three. What we can hand you instead is a finished shop you can use this afternoon.

faqs.q: I opened two months ago with no reviews. Where does this start?
faqs.a: With the Google listing, because it's the quickest thing to fix and the first thing anybody looks at. Verified, categorized, photographed and filled in properly, it can start doing work within weeks. Reviews build behind it once every customer is being asked automatically instead of occasionally.

faqs.q: Is a website worth it before I've got regulars?
faqs.a: That's exactly when it earns most. Regulars don't need a website, they need you to be open. The site is for the person who has never heard of you and is choosing between three shops in the time a light takes to change.

faqs.q: What does this cost a shop that just opened?

pages.metaDescription: Order-ahead websites, lunch menus and catering pages for restaurants in Lombard, IL, built for the office trade and the takeout rush at twenty to twelve.
pages.h1: Websites, takeout ordering and lunch menus for restaurants in Lombard, IL.
pages.lede: Lunch is a twenty-minute decision, made by somebody who has already left their desk in their head. Whoever can be ordered from in four taps takes the money.

sections.h2: The lunch order gets placed at twenty to twelve, and it gets placed once.
paras: There's a narrow band in the late morning where an office decides. Somebody says they're going out, two other people put in a request, and one person ends up holding a phone. If your food can be ordered and paid for in that minute, you're in. If it needs a call to a line that's already busy, the decision moves on without you and nobody feels bad about it.

Order-ahead exists for exactly that minute. The ticket arrives before the customer does, the kitchen sees it while there's still time to time it, and the bag is on the counter when they walk in with fourteen minutes left of their break.

sections.h2: A pickup time is a promise, so let the kitchen set it.
paras: The worst version of takeout is a customer standing by the register at ten past twelve watching a kitchen that hasn't started their order. It costs you the next visit and it clogs the front of house during the only hour that pays.

Ordering on your own site lets you set how many orders a slot can hold and how long each one really needs, so the times you offer are times you can hit. Slow it down at the peak, open it back up at one. The customer would far rather be told twenty minutes and get twenty minutes than be told ten and stand there for nineteen.
bullets: Pickup slots capped to what the line can genuinely produce
Payment taken at the time of the order rather than at the counter
The whole menu readable and orderable on a phone in one hand
A confirmation with the time and the address, sent the moment it lands

sections.h2: Your Tuesday hours are the ones that cost you money.
paras: Weekend hours get checked and corrected because that's when owners are looking. Weekday lunch hours drift. A holiday that half the offices take, a week you open late, the day the kitchen starts at eleven instead of half ten — those are the ones that end with somebody standing at a locked door at 11:40 with eight coworkers waiting on a text.

So the hours on your site and on your Google listing are ours to keep straight, including the odd weeks and the days that move. Send a message and it changes. That's what a couple of updates a month is for, and most owners spend them on exactly this.

sections.h2: A tray for twelve is a different order and deserves its own page.
paras: Somebody organizing lunch for a meeting is not shopping for lunch. They want to know how far ahead you need notice, what feeds twelve without going soggy, whether it turns up hot, what it costs per head and whether you'll bring it upstairs. Buried in a line at the bottom of the menu, that request either never gets made or arrives as a phone call with none of the details in it.

Give it a page and a form of its own. Ask for the date, the headcount, the building and the time it has to be on the table. You'll field fewer enquiries and quote more of the ones worth having, and the person ordering will notice that you've clearly done this before.

sections.h2: The office that ordered once is the easiest sale you'll ever make again.
paras: Individual customers are hard to keep track of. An office isn't. It's one name, one email address and a standing habit of feeding a dozen people every few weeks, usually decided by the same person each time.

Once that's written down, the follow-up is obvious and cheap. A note in November about holiday trays. A message in the spring saying the summer menu is on. It reads as helpful because it is, and it goes to somebody who has already tasted the food and liked it enough to be responsible for it in front of colleagues.

sections.h2: The two plans, and where ordering sits.
paras: Foundation is the getting-found half at $250 a month, with a one-time $250 to build it — the site on your own domain, the Google Business Profile, booking against your calendar, email at your own address and the search work behind all of it.

Taking money online lives on Growth, which is $500 a month with a one-time $500. That's where ordering and payment, the guest ledger, the automatic messages, expense tracking, the monthly report and the accounting sync switch on. Twelve months either way, billed the same date each month, and a year settled in advance is 15 percent lighter — $2,550 or $5,100, with the build billed on its own. Call answering runs $100 a month if the phone is the thing beating you.

sections.h2: Put an order through Knox Guac at lunchtime.
paras: Knox Guac is a taqueria with the ordering switched on, built by us end to end. Order something, watch the confirmation arrive, then open the ledger behind it and find the same ticket sitting there with your name on it.

pages.townPara: The village runs up against I-88 along its southern edge, and the research-and-development office corridor there keeps a weekday population in Lombard that may not sleep here at all. They arrive around eight, they eat somewhere between eleven and one, and by six those same buildings have gone dark. It's a lunch economy with a hard edge at both ends of the day. A kitchen that can be ordered from before anyone stands up from a desk takes a share of it. A kitchen reachable only by phone, during the exact half hour it's least able to answer one, does not.

crmCallout.heading: Your regular here is a company, not a person.
crmCallout.para: A CRM is a plain filing cabinet for customers, orders and money, kept on a screen instead of on a spike by the pass. For a lunch kitchen that means remembering the office that ordered fourteen plates in March, who placed it, what they picked and what it came to. That list is who the catering menu goes to in November, and it's worth more than advertising, because every name on it has already eaten your food.

cta.heading: Order from a kitchen we built.
cta.para: Four minutes with the demo will tell you more than the rest of this page did. Nobody rings you afterwards unless you ask us to.

faqs.q: Can customers order and pay for pickup on my own site?
faqs.a: Yes, on Growth. The order arrives with the items, the pickup time and the payment already taken, and it lands in the same ledger as everything else. The money goes into your account rather than being split with a platform first.

faqs.q: Can I limit how many orders come in at once?
faqs.a: You set what a pickup slot holds and how long each order needs. At the peak of the rush the times on offer stretch out on their own, then come back in when the line clears. It stops the kitchen being sold a minute it doesn't have.

faqs.q: We only really trade at lunch on weekdays. Is this still worth it?
faqs.a: It's arguably worth more, because a short trading window punishes every missed order twice. The hours have to be exactly right, the ordering has to work one-handed, and the catering enquiry from an office has to reach you the day it's typed rather than the day you check voicemail.

pages.formSub: Tell us how orders reach you now and we'll show you the same rush arriving differently.

pages.title: Auto Repair Websites, Lombard IL | Project Knox
pages.metaDescription: Websites, online booking and seasonal service reminders for auto repair shops in Lombard, IL. Have the appointment book ready for the first frost.
pages.h1: Websites and seasonal service reminders for auto repair shops in Lombard, IL.
pages.lede: This trade runs on a calendar, and most shops read it about a week late. The first hard frost and the first genuinely hot afternoon each fill a bay for a fortnight, and both are coming whether the book is ready or not.

sections.h2: The first cold morning books itself, and you can see it coming.
paras: One night the temperature drops and by seven the next morning the phone is going: no-starts, tire pressure lights, a heater blowing cold, a battery that was fine in September and is done now. Every shop in town has the same morning. The difference is whether you spend it triaging strangers or working through people you already wrote to last week.

The week before is when that message should go out, and it doesn't need to be clever. A note to the customers whose batteries you last tested a couple of winters ago, offering a check before the weather turns, fills the days that would otherwise be spent turning cars away.

sections.h2: Tires get planned right up until the moment nobody is planning anything.
paras: Almost everyone knows their tires are getting on. They intend to deal with it, and the intention survives until a wet Thursday or a sidewall that gives up in a pothole, at which point it becomes an emergency at somebody else's shop because that shop could get them in.

You already measured the tread at the last oil change. Written down against the vehicle, that measurement becomes a message in October worth real money — the largest single ticket plenty of drivers ever buy from you, sold calmly, in a week you chose, instead of frantically in a week you didn't.
bullets: Tread and battery readings recorded against the plate, not on a copy that goes home in the glovebox
Reminders that go out by mileage as well as by date
A seasonal note before the weather, not during it
Declined work kept on a list with the date it was quoted

sections.h2: The maintenance calendar is a list you already own.
paras: Every car through your bays leaves behind a date, a mileage and a set of intervals. Most shops keep all three and then never use them, because using them means somebody sitting down on a Friday with a stack of invoices and a phone.

It's the same work done automatically. Oil at the interval you set. Fluids, filters, the inspection due before a plate renewal. The customer gets a message that reads like it came from the counter, taps once and takes a slot. Nobody in the building had to remember anything, and the quick-lube by the highway doesn't get the visit.

sections.h2: A seasonal spike only hurts the shop it surprises.
paras: Two weeks of chaos followed by three flat ones is the shape of the year in this trade, and the flat weeks are where the money actually goes missing. If you can see the spike coming you can order parts ahead of it, staff it properly, and push the routine work into the weeks either side of it.

Online booking helps more than owners expect here, because it spreads demand instead of concentrating it into whoever gets through on the phone first. People will happily take next Tuesday at eight if next Tuesday at eight is visible. They just won't hold for six minutes to find out whether it exists.

sections.h2: A driver who only turns up when something breaks can be put on a schedule.
paras: Reactive customers are exhausting and unprofitable. They arrive in a panic, they compare you against two other shops, and you never see them again until the next failure, which might be at somebody else's counter.

The way that changes is unglamorous. You tell them what's due and when, in writing, before it's urgent. After the second or third time somebody is contacted a week ahead rather than rescued on a Monday, they stop shopping around, because being looked after is the thing they actually wanted and nobody else was offering it.

sections.h2: Both prices, on the page where you can see them.
paras: Foundation costs $250 monthly and $250 the once: website on a domain you own, the Google Business Profile set up properly, booking on your own calendar, email at your address, the local search work, plus a couple of changes a month for the asking.

Growth costs $500 monthly and $500 the once, and brings the customer and vehicle ledger, automatic review requests, the reminder messages this whole page is about, card payments, expense tracking, monthly reporting and the accounting sync. A year paid in one go is 15 percent less — $2,550 or $5,100, setup handled separately. Round-the-clock answering is $100 a month, review replies $130, and anything unusual gets quoted to the job in writing first.

sections.h2: Book a job into Knox Knocks and watch it land.
paras: Knox Knocks is a repair shop we built from the domain outward. Take an appointment on it as a driver would, then look at the record that appointment created on the other side of the counter.

pages.townPara: Butterfield Road, which is also 22nd Street and IL 56, runs along the south of the village and carries the sort of daily mileage that wears a car out on a schedule. Every vehicle on it is accumulating the same three things — cycles on a battery, miles on a set of tires, hours on a set of pads. None of that arrives as a surprise. It arrives as a season. The shop that wrote to those drivers in the week before the frost isn't the shop they're ringing in a panic on the morning after it.

crmCallout.heading: Every car you've touched is a date sitting in a calendar.
crmCallout.para: Behind the abbreviation there's nothing clever: it's the record of who you serve, what you did and when it comes round again. Mileage, last service, the tread you measured in September, the brake job somebody put off in June. Once that lives against the vehicle rather than in a folder, the seasonal messages send themselves and reach the people who genuinely need them, which is the only sort anybody reads.

cta.heading: See what a full book in November looks like.
cta.para: Open the demo shop, run an appointment through it, then take the ledger apart and look at how a reminder gets built. Questions reach a person on (331) 291-7400.

faqs.q: Can reminders go out on mileage instead of dates?
faqs.a: Both, and you pick which suits the job. An oil interval works on estimated mileage, an inspection works on a date, and a seasonal check works on the week of the year you choose. They all come from the same record, so a customer never gets three of them in a fortnight.

faqs.q: How do I keep the first cold week from turning into chaos?
faqs.a: By starting the week before it. Contact the customers whose batteries and tires you already have readings for, open extra bookable slots ahead of the drop, and let people take a time online rather than queue on the phone. The demand is the same either way. What changes is whether it arrives spread out or all at once.

faqs.q: What does this cost a shop that's flat out half the year?
faqs.a: $250 a month plus $250 at the start for the site, profile, booking and search work, or $500 a month plus $500 for the plan carrying the ledger, the reminders, the payments and the reports. The bill is the same in the flat months, and the flat months are precisely when the reminder list earns it back.

pages.formHeading: Which two weeks of the year break you?
pages.formSub: Name them and we'll show you what going into those weeks with a full book would take.

pages.h1: Websites and group booking for nail salons in Lombard, IL.
pages.lede: One woman booking a fill is a fifteen-second decision. Six women booking for a wedding on the same Saturday morning is a logistics problem, and it usually reaches you as a text sent to somebody's cousin.

sections.h2: A party of six is four chairs and a lot of arithmetic.
paras: Two of them want a full set, one wants gel toes as well, one is fifteen and only needs a paint, and they all have to be at a church by one. Solving that on the phone takes eleven minutes and a pencil, and you solve it again three days later when one of them drops out and her sister takes the slot.

It's the same puzzle every time, which means it can be handled as a form instead of a conversation. Names, the service each person wants, the time everyone has to be finished by. Once that arrives written down, staggering the starts across the chairs you actually have takes a minute rather than a lunch break.
bullets: One request covering several people, with a service against each name
Start times staggered across technicians automatically
A finish-by time captured before anything gets confirmed
A confirmation to each person's own phone, not just to the organizer

sections.h2: Whoever books is almost never whoever sits down.
paras: A mother books for a daughter and two friends. A bridesmaid books for the bride. A woman books for her mother's birthday and won't be there herself. So the contact details you take belong to the organizer, and the reminders need to reach the people in the chairs, and confusing the two is how a party turns up with half its members missing.

Both get held on the same record. The organizer gets the money and the messages about the money. Everybody else gets a reminder the day before with their own name and time on it, which is the difference between six people arriving together and six people trickling in over forty minutes.

sections.h2: Occasion work is decided months before the appointment.
paras: Nobody arranges a wedding morning three days out. The searching happens in winter for a date in June, and it happens at night, on a phone, by somebody with a list of things to sort out and a mild fear of getting one of them wrong.

Which means there needs to be something for her to find. A page about group bookings that says how many you can take at once, how early you need the date, whether you open ahead of hours for a party, and what a bridal morning actually looks like in your room. Salons that publish that get asked. Salons that don't get skipped, quietly, without ever knowing it happened.

sections.h2: A deposit is what turns six names into six chairs.
paras: Group bookings collapse in a way single appointments never do — one person cancels, the shape of it changes, and by Friday you're holding a Saturday morning for three people instead of six. That morning was the most valuable inventory you had and it can't be resold at short notice.

Taking a deposit at the moment of agreement fixes most of it, and nobody has ever been offended by being asked. A card goes through on your own site, it sits against the booking, and the balance settles on the day. Payments come with Growth, at $500 a month plus a one-time $500.

sections.h2: Gift cards are the occasion nobody plans for.
paras: Mother's Day, birthdays, the thank-you for someone who helped out, the December week where every second customer is buying for somebody else. Sold on the site they cost you nothing to stock, they get paid for today and redeemed in February, and they bring in a person who might never have chosen you on her own.

The part that matters is what happens after the redemption. That woman is now somebody with a name, a service and a date, sitting in your book like any other client, and the messages that go to everybody else go to her too.

sections.h2: What both plans run to.
paras: Foundation is $250 a month with a one-time $250 build: the website on your own domain, the Google Business Profile done properly, booking wired into the calendar you already keep, email at your own address, the local SEO and two updates a month.

Growth is $500 a month with a one-time $500 build, and adds the client ledger, deposits and card payments, the automatic reminders and review requests, expense tracking, the monthly report and a clean handoff to your accounting software. Both are twelve-month partnerships on a fixed billing date. A year up front is 15 percent off, which works out to $212.50 or $425 a month, with the build charged separately.

sections.h2: Book into Knox Nails and see the reminder arrive.
paras: Knox Nails takes real bookings and sends real confirmations, so run yourself through it as a client would and see what turns up on the phone afterwards.

pages.townPara: Lilac Time takes over the first three weeks of May and turns the village into somewhere people travel to, and the Lilac Parade closes Main Street between Central and Parkside. Ranged around those weeks is everything else that puts a group of women in one room on one morning — the graduations, the weddings booked a year out, prom, the family photographs somebody has been arranging since February. Salons tend to experience all of it as a rush. It behaves far better as a calendar, and the whole difference is whether those bookings were taken in March or fielded on a Thursday afternoon.

crmCallout.heading: One booking, six people, one record.
crmCallout.para: CRM sounds like software and behaves like a desk diary that never loses a page. A group booking sits in it as a single job with six names underneath, the deposit against it and the service each person chose. Come the following spring it can tell you which families were in for a wedding last May, which is a message worth sending in March. It also holds the gift cards sold in December that still haven't been used.

cta.heading: Try it as the woman organizing everybody.
cta.para: Go through the demo as though you were booking for a group, then look at how it lands on the salon's side. If the shape of it fits your Saturdays, we'll build yours the same way.

faqs.q: Can somebody book a whole party in one go?
faqs.a: Yes. One request holds several people with a service against each name and a time everyone has to be finished by, and the starts get staggered across whoever is working. The organizer handles the money and each person gets her own reminder.

faqs.q: Can I take a deposit for a group booking?
faqs.a: You can, on Growth. Set what the deposit is, take it on the card at the moment the booking is agreed, and settle the balance on the day. It's the cheapest protection there is for a Saturday morning you can't resell.

faqs.q: Can gift cards be sold through the website?
faqs.a: They can, and it's one of the few things that pays for itself before anybody walks in. They're bought online, redeemed against a booking later, and the person who redeems one becomes a client in the book like everybody else.

pages.h1: Websites and referral pages for chiropractors in Lombard, IL.
pages.lede: A good share of any practice arrives because somebody else pointed at you — a trainer, a massage therapist, a physical therapist two doors down. That's a relationship, and relationships leave no trace unless something writes them down.

sections.h2: The people who could send you patients are standing in front of them all day.
paras: A trainer watches somebody's shoulder every Tuesday. A massage therapist has an hour of quiet conversation with a person who mentions their neck. A running club has three members limping. None of those are competitors and all of them are asked, regularly, whether they know anybody good.

What decides the answer is rarely skill, because they can't assess yours. It's whether you're easy to describe, easy to look up and quick to fit somebody in. A therapist will send a client to the practice she can explain in one sentence and be confident won't embarrass her.

sections.h2: A referral partner needs something to point at.
paras: Sending somebody your way means saying a name and hoping it sticks until they get home. It sticks far better if there's a page she can hand over — what you treat, what a first appointment involves, how soon somebody can be seen and what you'll send back to her afterwards.
That page isn't written for patients and shouldn't read like it. It's written for a professional deciding whether to attach her own reputation to yours, and the things she cares about are specific.
bullets: What you treat and, just as usefully, what you don't
How quickly a new referral can be seen this week
Whether you report back to the person who sent them
A direct way to reach you that isn't the patient booking line

sections.h2: Saying no out loud is how you get sent the next one.
paras: Some people who walk in should be somewhere else — imaging first, a physician first, a surgical opinion, something that isn't yours to treat. Every practitioner knows this and not every practice says it anywhere a stranger can read it.

Putting it in writing does two things at once. A nervous patient reads it as confidence, because somebody prepared to turn work away is somebody with a line. And another professional reads it as safety, which is the entire basis on which she decides whether to send you her clients. Publishing your limits is, awkwardly, one of the better ways to grow.

sections.h2: Ask where they came from, and write it down the same day.
paras: Most practices can name their top referrer and are guessing about the rest. That guess costs money, because it decides who gets the thank-you, who gets a visit, and which relationships quietly go cold without anybody noticing.

One field on the intake, filled in at the desk or by the patient before they arrive, and a year later you know exactly which gym, which therapist and which neighbour has been carrying you. Then you can be properly grateful to the right people instead of generally grateful to everybody.

sections.h2: Referrals go stale faster than anyone expects.
paras: A relationship that fed you four patients last spring can produce nothing this spring for reasons as small as a staff change or a card that fell off a noticeboard. Nobody fell out. It just stopped.

A short note twice a year to everybody who has ever sent someone your way is enough to keep it alive, and it's the sort of task that never happens by intention. Sitting on a list with dates against it, it happens on a Tuesday morning in ten minutes.

sections.h2: The cost, stated the same way we'd state it on the phone.
paras: Foundation is $250 a month after a one-time $250: the website on a domain in the practice's name, the Google Business Profile, online scheduling on your calendar, email at your own address, the local search work and a couple of updates a month.

Growth is $500 a month after a one-time $500 and adds the ledger where the referral source lives, automated reminders and recall, review requests, online payment, expense tracking, monthly reports and the accounting sync. Twelve months, one date, one bill. Settle the year in advance and it's $2,550 or $5,100, with the build fee separate. There is no larger plan being kept back for bigger practices.

sections.h2: Walk through Knox Pops before you ask us anything.
paras: Knox Pops is a practice we built end to end. Book a first visit on it, then look at how that booking appears behind the desk and what the follow-up would have done next.

pages.townPara: Downtown Lombard is a tight grid where Main Street crosses St. Charles Road, filled in by Park, Parkside and Central Avenues, with Lombard Town Centre working those blocks from 2 S. Park Ave. Practitioners sit close together in a district that size, and so do the people best placed to send you patients — the studio upstairs, the therapist across the road, the trainer whose clients all live within a mile. Proximity on its own doesn't make a referral network. Being easy to describe, quick to find and able to see somebody this week is what makes one.

crmCallout.heading: Where a patient came from belongs in the file.
crmCallout.para: Reduced to plain English, a CRM is the address book, the appointment book and the money book kept as one thing. Add a single field to it — who sent this person — and within a year you know which relationships are genuinely feeding the practice and which are only friendly. The same ledger carries the recall list, the unpaid invoices and the enquiry that never became a booking. Clinical notes stay in whatever you chart in.

cta.heading: Open the practice we built and use it properly.
cta.para: Nothing on it is a picture of a working thing, and nobody is going to chase you afterwards. If you'd like to talk once you've looked, a real person writes back inside a day.

faqs.q: Can we see which referral source a patient came from?
faqs.a: Yes, and it's one field rather than a project. It gets captured at intake, sits on the patient record, and adds up over the year into a plain list of who is actually sending people. Most practices are surprised by the middle of that list.

faqs.q: Should we really publish what we don't treat?
faqs.a: In our experience it wins more than it costs. Patients read a clear scope as confidence rather than as a limitation, and other practitioners read it as the reason it's safe to send you their clients. It also spares your front desk conversations that were never going to end in an appointment.

faqs.q: What does a practice pay for this?
faqs.a: $250 a month plus $250 once for the site, profile, scheduling, email and SEO. $500 a month plus $500 once for the version that also holds the patient ledger, the recall messaging, the payments and the reports. Paying twelve months ahead takes 15 percent off either.

pages.title: Snow & Lawn Contract Sites, Lombard IL | Project Knox
pages.metaDescription: Websites, snow contracts, per-push billing and off-season follow-up for lawn and landscape crews in Lombard, IL. Sign the winter in September.
pages.h1: Websites, snow contracts and off-season work for lawn and landscape crews in Lombard, IL.
pages.lede: January's money was agreed in September. By the time a forecast makes the news the routes are full, and the only thing left to sell is a very long night.

sections.h2: Snow is sold in September and delivered in January.
paras: Every customer who signs in autumn is a customer who isn't ringing round in a panic in December, and every one who doesn't sign is a gap you'll fill at three in the morning with somebody you've never worked for. The selling window is short, it's early, and it opens while your crews are still cutting grass.

Which is why it can't depend on you having a free evening. The renewal goes out to last winter's list on a date you set, the new enquiries come in through a page written for winter rather than a paragraph tacked on to the mowing site, and the agreement gets read and returned online instead of being carried around in a truck for a fortnight.

sections.h2: Per push or seasonal is the entire conversation, so put it on the page.
paras: Homeowners and property managers are weighing two different bets and most of them don't know the terms. One pays for each visit, one pays a flat amount for the winter and transfers the risk to you. Both are reasonable and both get chosen for different reasons.

Explaining that in writing does the arguing for you in advance. What depth brings the truck out. Whether salt is included or billed on its own. What happens in a winter with almost no snow, and what happens in one with far too much. Say it plainly and you'll have a shorter conversation in September and no conversation at all in March.
bullets: The trigger depth written down where anybody can read it
Salt and ice melt priced clearly, not left to be discovered on an invoice
What a visit includes — drive, walks, the space in front of the door
How a mild winter and a brutal one each get billed

sections.h2: At four in the morning, nobody calls twice.
paras: The phone at that hour is a property manager who needs a lot cleared before staff arrive, and if it rings out she calls the next number on her list and you never learn it happened. You were asleep, which is entirely reasonable, and it cost you a contract anyway.

The answering bolt-on is $100 a month and it picks up at that hour, takes the address and the detail, and leaves it written down and waiting for you. Going the other way, one message to a route the night before — we're on tonight, expect us around five — stops thirty separate phone calls before they start.

sections.h2: Eight months a year you're not the snow guy, and they forget.
paras: A customer who only ever sees you when it's white outside has no reason to think of you in April, even if you'd happily do the mulch, the cleanup and the cutting. That's not disloyalty. You simply never came up.

So the list works both directions. The people who take a seasonal contract hear from you in the spring about the beds and the first cut. The mowing customers hear from you in September about the driveway. It's the same handful of names, worked twice, and it's how a business stops having two separate customer bases that don't know they overlap.

sections.h2: Winter invoicing goes wrong in ways summer invoicing doesn't.
paras: Per-push work generates a pile of small invoices in a fortnight, all of them for visits made in the dark, some of them disputed a month later by somebody who genuinely can't remember whether you came on the fourteenth.

Invoicing the same day, from the truck, with the date and the property on it, settles almost all of that before it starts. Seasonal contracts get billed on an even schedule so the money isn't all in one month, cards on file take care of the rest, and what's outstanding is a screen you can look at rather than a thing you worry about at the yard.

sections.h2: The whole cost of it, both plans.
paras: Foundation: $250 every month, plus $250 once at the start. That's the site on a domain registered to you, the Google Business Profile built out, booking that writes to your own calendar, email at your own domain, the search work for the towns you cover, and two updates a month for the asking.

Growth: $500 every month, plus $500 once. On top of everything above it carries the property and contract ledger, quoting and invoicing, the automatic messages, card payments, expenses against each job, monthly reports and the sync to QuickBooks. Twelve months on a fixed date, 15 percent off if the year goes in at once, and review replies available at $130 a month if you want them handled.

sections.h2: Send yourself a snow enquiry in Knox Blocks.
paras: Knox Blocks is a working landscape business we built the whole way through. Put a request through it, then follow it into the ledger and see what a crew would be looking at on a Tuesday.

pages.townPara: Lilacia Park at 150 S. Park Avenue exists because Colonel William Plum left the village his garden in 1927, along with something close to two hundred varieties of lilac. It's a public park that grew out of one man's patience with plants that do nothing at all for most of the year. That's worth holding on to in a village nicknamed after a flower — people here notice ground that's been looked after, and they notice it in May on the strength of work done the previous autumn. Snow contracts run on exactly the same logic, signed in one season and judged in another.

crmCallout.heading: One list that knows who's on the route and who's only on the lawn.
crmCallout.para: The word covers something entirely ordinary — every customer, every property and every dollar written in one place you can search. For a crew working both seasons that means knowing which properties are under a seasonal contract, which are per push, what each is billed and what's been paid. In September it hands you the list to write to. At four in the morning it tells you the order to drive in.

cta.heading: Get the winter sold before the leaves are down.
cta.para: Take the demo apart, then tell us how many properties you plough and how many you cut. We'll come back with what we'd build and what it costs, in writing.

faqs.q: Can customers agree a snow contract through the website?
faqs.a: Yes. The terms sit on a page they can read without ringing you, the enquiry arrives with the property address on it, and the agreement goes out and comes back without anybody driving anywhere. That matters most in the two weeks of autumn when everybody decides at once.

faqs.q: Can it handle per-push and seasonal accounts together?
faqs.a: It has to, because almost every crew runs both. Per-push properties get invoiced per visit with the date and the work on them, seasonal accounts get billed on an even schedule through the winter, and both sit in the same ledger with a card on file if the customer wants one.

faqs.q: How much of this is on the $250 plan?
faqs.a: The website, the Google Business Profile, booking on your calendar, email at your own domain and the SEO — enough to be found and to take an enquiry. Contracts, invoicing, payments, the automatic messages and the reports are on the $500 plan, and that's the half that earns its keep in a busy February.

pages.formHeading: How many properties do you plough?
pages.formSub: Send that number alongside your mowing count and we'll show you what one list holding both would look like.
